reasons: The lake identity record names Maryland v. Garrison, U.S. Supreme Court, decided 1987-02-24, year 1987.
The lake citation fields match the asserted official citation, vendor-neutral citation, and parallel citations: 480 U.S. 79; 1987 U.S. LEXIS 559; 107 S. Ct. 1013; 94 L. Ed. 2d 72; 55 U.S.L.W. 4190.
The opinion expressly frames the case around the Warrant Clause's requirement of particularly describing the place to be searched.
The holding refines particularity doctrine for a warrant that became overbroad only because of a reasonable latent factual mistake about the premises.
residual_risks: The role label is partly classificatory, but the disclosed opinion text and lake progeny/citation fields support treating the case as important to the Particularity home.

defect.evidence_quote: subjective good-faith belief would not in itself justify either the arrest or the subsequent search.
defect.problem: The warrant-validity point is supported, but the holding's 'reasonable, good-faith mistake...' phrasing should not imply subjective good faith is enough; the opinion requires an objectively understandable and reasonable mistake.
defect.proposed_fix: Revise to: "A warrant's validity is judged on the information reasonably available when it issued; a search based on a mistaken understanding of the premises is valid only where the officers' failure to realize the overbreadth was objectively understandable and reasonable."

reasons: The opinion states that later-discovered facts do not retroactively invalidate a warrant valid when issued.
The opinion states that the search depended on whether the officers' failure to realize overbreadth was objectively understandable and reasonable.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Replace 'good-faith mistake' with 'objectively understandable and reasonable mistake' to track the holding.
